questions.stem: After a busy day in a surgical suite and on a medical unit, the sterile processing and environmental services teams review how four items should be cleaned between clients. For each item, indicate the required level of processing.

rows.text: Surgical instruments that enter sterile tissue
A flexible endoscope that touches mucous membranes
A blood pressure cuff used on intact skin
Surfaces in the room of a client with C. difficile

rationale.correct: Spaulding classification: critical items are sterilized, semi-critical items get high-level disinfection and non-critical items get low-level disinfection; C. difficile needs sporicidal cleaning.

perOption.r1:c1: Critical items that enter sterile tissue must be sterilized.
perOption.r2:c1: Often not possible for heat-sensitive scopes.
perOption.r4:c4: Spores need sporicidal agents such as bleach.

references: CDC infection control and isolation precautions guidance

questions.educationalObjective: Choose the level of cleaning and disinfection.

questions.stem: A tube of blood breaks and spills on the floor of a client's room. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Wipe it up with a wet paper towel and throw the towel in the trash
Put on gloves, absorb it, then use an approved disinfectant
Cover the spill with a towel and wait for housekeeping to arrive later
Mop the floor with plenty of plain water to dilute the blood quickly

rationale.correct: Blood spills: wear gloves, contain and absorb, clean with an approved disinfectant and dispose of waste as biohazard.

perOption.a: Blood spills need protective equipment and disinfection.
perOption.b: Gloves protect the nurse, and disinfection kills bloodborne organisms.

references: CDC infection control and isolation precautions guidance

questions.stem: During influenza season, which measures help prevent spread of influenza on a medical unit? Select all that apply.

options.text: Offering yearly influenza vaccine to staff
Asking staff with fever and cough to stay home
Giving masks to visitors who are coughing
Placing clients with influenza on droplet precautions
Letting sick staff work if they wear gloves
Keeping clients with and without influenza in the same room

rationale.correct: Influenza prevention: staff vaccination, sick staff staying home, masking coughing visitors, droplet precautions and cohorting.

perOption.e: Gloves do not stop respiratory spread.
perOption.f: Clients with influenza should be separated or cohorted together.

references: CDC infection control and isolation precautions guidance

questions.educationalObjective: Prevent influenza spread on a unit.

questions.stem: An infection prevention nurse observes a nurse caring for a client. Highlight the moments when hand hygiene was needed but missed.

segments.text: enters the room and adjusts the client's IV pump without cleaning the hands
cleans the hands, then puts on gloves to empty the urine bag
. After emptying the bag, the nurse
removes the gloves and goes straight to straighten the bed linens
cleans the hands at the door

rationale.correct: The five moments of hand hygiene: before touching a client, before clean or aseptic procedures, after body fluid exposure, after touching a client and after touching the client's surroundings.

perOption.s2: Hand hygiene is needed before touching the client or the client's surroundings.
perOption.s6: Hand hygiene is needed after glove removal and body fluid exposure.

references: CDC infection control and isolation precautions guidance

questions.stem: An older mercury thermometer breaks in a home health client's bathroom, spilling small beads of mercury on the tile floor. What should the nurse advise?

options.text: Vacuum the beads up right away so they do not spread across the floor
Ventilate the room and collect the beads with a spill kit
Sweep the beads into the regular trash with a broom and dustpan
Wash the beads down the bathroom drain with hot water

rationale.correct: Small mercury spills: clear the area, ventilate, collect with a spill kit or stiff paper, seal and dispose as hazardous waste; never vacuum or sweep.

perOption.a: Vacuuming spreads mercury vapor into the air.
perOption.b: Mercury is collected carefully and disposed of as hazardous waste; vacuuming and sweeping spread vapor.
perOption.c: Sweeping breaks beads apart and contaminates the broom.
perOption.d: Mercury in the drain contaminates the water system.

references: Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)

questions.stem: Two nurses are moving a client who cannot help from the bed to a stretcher using a friction-reducing sheet. Place the steps in order.

items.text: Lock the wheels of the bed and stretcher
Position the friction-reducing sheet under the client
Raise the bed to the height of the stretcher and lower the side rails
Move the client across on a coordinated count

rationale.correct: Lateral transfers: lock wheels, level the surfaces, use a friction-reducing device and move together on a count.

questions.stem: Two clients on the same unit are named Maria Lopez and Mario Lopes. Which action best prevents a mix-up?

options.text: Use room numbers to tell the clients apart when giving medications
Use a name alert and two identifiers at each contact
Move one client to another unit to avoid confusion
Call each client by first name to keep things simple for the staff

rationale.correct: For clients with similar names, use name alerts and two identifiers every time; never use room numbers.

perOption.b: Name alerts and two identifiers, such as name and date of birth, prevent errors.
perOption.c: Not necessary and may disrupt care.
perOption.d: First names alone are not reliable identifiers.

references: NCSBN National Guidelines for Nursing Delegation; LaCharity, Prioritization, Delegation & Assignment

questions.stem: A thin, confused older client has full-length side rails raised on a hospital bed. The nurse finds the client's head and neck caught between the mattress and the side rail. What hazard does this show?

options.text: A pressure injury from lying too long on one side
Bed entrapment in a gap between the mattress and rail
A fall caused by the bed being left in a high position
An electrical hazard from the bed controls

rationale.correct: Bed entrapment occurs in gaps between the mattress, rails and frame; confused, frail clients are at highest risk. Use correctly sized mattresses, partial rails and close observation.

perOption.a: This is an entrapment hazard, not a pressure injury.
perOption.b: Gaps between rails and mattresses can trap the head, neck or chest and cause death.
perOption.d: This is a mechanical entrapment hazard.

references: Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)

questions.stem: In a busy pediatric unit, a nurse is teaching parents how children's emotional needs change as they grow, so that care in the hospital supports each child's stage. For each age group, indicate the developmental task described by Erikson.

rationale.correct: Erikson: trust (infant), autonomy (toddler), initiative (preschool), industry (school age), identity (adolescent).

perOption.r1:c1: Infants learn trust when needs are met.
perOption.r3:c3: Preschoolers start activities and imagine roles.
perOption.r4:c4: Adolescents form a sense of identity.

references: Pediatric nursing texts (e.g. Hockenberry, Wong's Essentials of Pediatric Nursing)

questions.stem: At a 2-week postpartum visit, a client says they cry easily, cannot sleep even when the baby sleeps and feel like a bad parent. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Tell the client these are the baby blues and will pass within a few days
Screen for postpartum depression with the Edinburgh scale
Suggest the client stop breastfeeding to get more sleep
Encourage the client to keep busy with the baby so the feelings go away

rationale.correct: Screen for postpartum depression with a validated tool when symptoms persist past 2 weeks or include guilt, insomnia or hopelessness.

perOption.a: Symptoms beyond 2 weeks with guilt and insomnia need screening.
perOption.b: Validated screening identifies depression and guides referral.
perOption.c: This does not address possible depression.
perOption.d: This dismisses symptoms that need assessment.

references: Maternal-newborn nursing texts (e.g. Perry; Lowdermilk)
Psychiatric-mental health nursing texts (e.g. Varcarolis; Halter)

questions.stem: The nurse is teaching new parents about safe infant sleep. Complete the sentences.

content.template: The baby should sleep on the {{b1}}, on a {{b2}} with no pillows, bumpers or blankets, and in the {{b3}}.

options.text: back
stomach
side
firm, flat mattress
soft pillow-top mattress
couch cushion
parents' room but in a separate crib or bassinet
parents' bed between the parents
nursery with the door closed

rationale.correct: Safe sleep: back to sleep, firm flat surface, no soft bedding, room sharing without bed sharing and no smoke exposure.

perOption.b1:a: Back sleeping lowers the risk of sudden infant death.
perOption.b1:c: Side sleeping is unstable and increases risk.
perOption.b3:a: Room sharing without bed sharing lowers risk.
perOption.b3:c: Room sharing is recommended for at least the first 6 months.

references: Pediatric nursing texts (e.g. Hockenberry, Wong's Essentials of Pediatric Nursing)

questions.stem: The parent of an 18-month-old who weighs 11 kg asks when to turn the car seat to face forward. What should the nurse advise?

options.text: Turn it forward now, since the child is over 1 year old
Keep it rear-facing until the seat's rear-facing limit
Turn it forward once the child's legs touch the back of the vehicle seat
Use a booster seat with the vehicle's lap and shoulder belt instead

rationale.correct: Keep children rear-facing as long as possible, until they reach the seat's rear-facing limits.

perOption.a: Age 1 is not the cutoff; rear-facing is safest as long as possible.
perOption.b: Children should ride rear-facing as long as the seat allows.
perOption.c: Leg contact is not a reason to turn forward.
perOption.d: Boosters are for older, larger children.

references: Pediatric nursing texts (e.g. Hockenberry, Wong's Essentials of Pediatric Nursing)

questions.stem: A healthy 16-year-old comes for a well visit. Which preventive services should the nurse expect? Select all that apply.

options.text: Screening for depression
A meningococcal vaccine booster
Confidential time alone with the provider
A screening colonoscopy for colorectal cancer
Questions about tobacco, vaping, alcohol and drugs
A routine screening mammogram
A dose of HPV vaccine if the series is not complete

rationale.correct: Adolescent visits include depression and substance use screening, confidential time, and vaccines such as the meningococcal booster at 16.

perOption.c: Supports honest discussion of risk behaviors.
perOption.g: HPV vaccination catches up through adolescence.

references: CDC/ACIP immunization schedules

questions.stem: A 66-year-old client who went through menopause at 51 and has never had a bone density test asks about osteoporosis screening. What should the nurse explain?

options.text: Screening is needed once a fracture has happened
A bone density (DXA) scan is advised for women 65 and older
A yearly x-ray of the spine is the best screening test
Screening is not needed if the client drinks milk each day

rationale.correct: Women 65 and older, and younger postmenopausal women at increased risk, should have DXA screening for osteoporosis.

perOption.a: Screening aims to find osteoporosis before a fracture.
perOption.b: Screening with DXA is recommended for women 65 and older and younger women at higher risk.
perOption.c: DXA, not plain x-ray, is the screening test.
perOption.d: Diet does not remove the need for screening.

references: U.S. Preventive Services Task Force recommendations

questions.stem: For each contraceptive method, choose the key teaching point.

options.text: Use a new condom for each act of intercourse
Use oil-based lubricant for comfort
Reuse it if it did not break
Take it at any time of day that is convenient
Take it at the same time each day
Skip a week whenever spotting occurs
Apply a new patch each week for 3 weeks, then a patch-free week
Apply one patch a month
Put the patch on the same spot each week
Insert the ring for 3 weeks, then remove it for 1 week
Remove the ring each night
Change the ring every day

rationale.correct: Teach correct use for each method: new condom each time, pills at the same time daily, weekly patches and a ring left in for 3 weeks.

questions.stem: A 31-year-old client at 16 weeks has a maternal serum screen showing an elevated alpha-fetoprotein (AFP) level. What should the nurse expect next?

options.text: No further testing, since screening results are usually wrong
A detailed ultrasound to check dating and the spine
Immediate delivery because the fetus is in danger
Starting high-dose folic acid now to reverse any defect

rationale.correct: An elevated AFP screen is followed by a detailed ultrasound and, if needed, further testing and counseling.

perOption.b: High AFP can come from wrong dates, twins, or neural tube or abdominal wall defects; ultrasound comes first.
perOption.c: An abnormal screen is not a reason for delivery.
perOption.d: Folic acid prevents but does not reverse neural tube defects.

references: Maternal-newborn nursing texts (e.g. Perry; Lowdermilk)

questions.stem: A client who has chosen not to breastfeed has painful, swollen breasts on the third day after birth. What should the nurse suggest?

options.text: Pump the breasts several times a day to relieve the fullness
Wear a supportive bra and use cold packs for comfort
Stand under a warm shower and let the water run over the breasts
Massage the breasts firmly several times a day

rationale.correct: For clients not breastfeeding: supportive bra, cold packs, mild analgesics and avoiding breast stimulation.

perOption.b: Support, cold and avoiding stimulation reduce engorgement in clients who are not breastfeeding.

questions.stem: A client admitted 3 days ago for a hip fracture drinks a fifth of vodka daily. Tonight the client is disoriented, picking at the air, seeing insects on the walls, sweating heavily and shaking. Temperature is 38.6 °C (101.5 °F), heart rate 132/min and blood pressure 178/104 mm Hg. Complete the diagram by placing the condition the client is most likely experiencing, 2 actions the nurse should take, and 2 parameters the nurse should monitor.

actions.text: Give benzodiazepines as prescribed using a symptom-based protocol
Give IV thiamine and fluids as prescribed
Apply four-point restraints as the first measure
Give haloperidol alone to stop the hallucinations
Keep the room dark and silent with the door closed

parameters.text: Vital signs and a withdrawal scale such as CIWA-Ar
Body weight measured once a week
Bowel sounds in each of the four quadrants
Color and clarity of the urine

rationale.correct: Delirium tremens is an emergency: benzodiazepines, thiamine before glucose, fluids, a safe calm environment and close monitoring of vital signs and seizures.

perOption.c1: Confusion, hallucinations, tremor, fever and autonomic instability 2 to 4 days after the last drink are delirium tremens.
perOption.c2: Infection can cause fever, but visual hallucinations and tremor in heavy drinkers on day 3 point to DTs.
perOption.c3: There is no history of dementia, and the autonomic signs fit withdrawal.
perOption.c4: Opioid withdrawal does not cause hallucinations and fever this high.
perOption.a1: Benzodiazepines treat withdrawal and prevent seizures.
perOption.a2: Thiamine prevents Wernicke encephalopathy, and fluids treat losses.
perOption.a3: Restraints increase agitation and injury; they are a last resort.
perOption.a4: Antipsychotics alone lower the seizure threshold and do not treat withdrawal.
perOption.a5: Dim, not dark, lighting and close observation are needed.

references: Psychiatric-mental health nursing texts (e.g. Varcarolis; Halter)
Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)

questions.stem: A client with a new diagnosis of terminal cancer makes these statements over several weeks. For each statement, indicate the stage of grief it best reflects.

rows.text: "The lab must have mixed up my results."
"Why me? I've taken care of myself my whole life!"
"If I can just see my grandchild graduate, I'll be ready."
"I've made my will and said what I needed to say to my family."

rationale.correct: Kübler-Ross stages (denial, anger, bargaining, depression, acceptance) do not always occur in order; nurses support clients wherever they are.

perOption.r1:c1: Refusing to believe the diagnosis is denial.
perOption.r3:c3: Seeking more time in exchange shows bargaining.

references: Psychiatric-mental health nursing texts (e.g. Varcarolis; Halter)
Written to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 20 November 2026.

questions.stem: A client with severe depression sits silently in the day room and answers questions with one word. What is the most therapeutic action?

options.text: Leave the client alone until they feel like talking to staff
Sit with the client quietly and use brief statements
Ask the client many questions to get them talking
Tell the client to cheer up and think about the good things in life

rationale.correct: With depressed, withdrawn clients, offer presence, short simple communication and small expectations.

perOption.b: Presence without pressure shows the client is worth the nurse's time.
perOption.c: Pressure to talk can overwhelm a depressed client.

references: Psychiatric-mental health nursing texts (e.g. Varcarolis; Halter)

questions.stem: Which factors increase a client's risk of postpartum depression? Select all that apply.

options.text: A history of depression
Little support from a partner or family
A stressful life event during pregnancy
An uncomplicated, planned pregnancy with strong support
Depression during pregnancy
Having a healthy term baby

rationale.correct: Risk factors for postpartum depression include past or prenatal depression, poor support, life stress and complications.

perOption.a: Past depression is a strong risk factor.

questions.stem: An 84-year-old client tells the nurse that a nephew who "helps with money" now controls the bank account. The client has unpaid bills, the electricity was recently shut off and the client says they are not allowed to see their statements. What should the nurse suspect?

options.text: Normal help from a trusted family member
Financial exploitation of the client
The early stages of dementia
Normal effects of retirement on income

rationale.correct: Financial exploitation signs include sudden loss of control of money, unpaid bills, unexplained withdrawals and blocked access; report as required.

perOption.a: Unpaid bills and blocked access suggest exploitation.
perOption.b: Loss of control over money, unpaid bills and blocked access are signs of financial abuse.
perOption.c: The concern is the nephew's control of money, not the client's memory.
perOption.d: This does not explain blocked access.

references: Psychiatric-mental health nursing texts (e.g. Varcarolis; Halter)
Written to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 20 November 2026.

questions.stem: During group therapy, one client keeps interrupting and talking about their own problems, and other members have stopped speaking. What should the nurse leading the group do?

options.text: Ignore the behavior so the client does not feel singled out
Thank the client, then invite other members to share
Ask the client to leave the group for the rest of the week
Let the group vote on whether the client can keep talking today

rationale.correct: Group leaders manage monopolizing members by acknowledging them, redirecting and setting limits to protect the group process.

perOption.a: Ignoring it lets the group become unproductive.
perOption.b: The leader redirects respectfully so the group can work for everyone.
perOption.c: Removal is not the first step.
perOption.d: This can embarrass the client and harm the group.

references: Psychiatric-mental health nursing texts (e.g. Varcarolis; Halter)

questions.stem: A nurse in an outpatient addiction clinic follows a client with alcohol use disorder over 2 years. Place the stages of change in the order the client would usually pass through them on the way to lasting sobriety.

items.text: Maintenance: has stayed sober for more than 6 months
Precontemplation: does not see a problem
Contemplation: thinks about changing but is unsure

rationale.correct: Transtheoretical model: precontemplation, contemplation, preparation, action and maintenance; interventions match the stage.
references: Psychiatric-mental health nursing texts (e.g. Varcarolis; Halter)

questions.stem: A client asks the nurse, "Would you pray with me before my surgery?" The nurse does not share the client's faith. What is the best response?

options.text: "I can't pray with you because we have different beliefs."
"I'll sit with you while you pray, and I can call the chaplain."
"Prayer won't affect how the surgery goes, so try to rest."
"Let's talk about the surgery instead to keep your mind busy before it starts."

rationale.correct: Support clients' spiritual needs by being present, respecting beliefs and offering chaplain or faith-leader support.

perOption.b: Being present and offering spiritual resources supports the client without the nurse imposing beliefs.

references: Psychiatric-mental health nursing texts (e.g. Varcarolis; Halter)
Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)
